analysis.one_liner: Bans for-profit prisons, caps jail phone and money-transfer fees, and ends family immigration detention.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to four House committees in February 2021, it sat in subcommittee until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would phase out privately run prisons and detention facilities within two years, putting confinement of prisoners and immigration detainees under direct government operation. It would cap phone calls from jails at a few cents a minute, ban the kickback-style 'site commissions' that phone companies pay to facilities, and put the consumer bureau in charge of fees that companies charge families to send money to jailed relatives. It would also require independent inspections of all immigration detention facilities, impose financial penalties for violations, and replace family detention with community-based case management run by nonprofits.
analysis.who_benefits: People in prisons, jails, and immigration detention, and their families, who currently pay high phone, video-call, and money-transfer fees; taxpayers, since contracts would no longer include a private profit margin; and asylum-seeking families, who could no longer be detained or separated.

how_it_helps.text: Phases out for-profit operation of federal, state, and local confinement facilities within two years, requiring core correctional services to be performed by government employees, with a one-year waiver in limited cases.

Caps prison phone rates at 4 cents per minute for debit or prepaid calls and 5 cents for collect calls, bans per-call connection fees and most ancillary fees, and bans site commissions paid by phone providers to confinement facilities.

Directs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to set standards ensuring fees for money transfers to people in jails and immigration detention are reasonable and proportional to the cost of the service.

Requires regular independent audits and ombudsman inspections of all facilities holding immigration detainees, makes detention contracts and audit records public, and mandates financial penalties and contract termination for facilities that repeatedly fail standards.

Prohibits detaining or separating family units apprehended by immigration authorities and replaces detention with community-based case management run by nonprofit organizations, while barring ankle-worn GPS monitors as an alternative.
Gives individuals a private right of action to sue over violations, with damages of at least $1,000 per violation and attorney fees for prevailing plaintiffs.

analysis.who_pays: Private prison and detention companies, prison phone and money-transfer providers, and state and local governments, which would assume direct operating costs, lose site commissions, and face new oversight and penalties in immigration detention.

drawbacks.text: State and local governments would have to bring confinement facilities under direct public operation within two years, a transition that could require hiring, training, and capital costs, with only a one-year waiver available.
The rate caps and fee bans are set against average industry cost data and a strict FCC rulemaking timeline; providers could cut services or litigate over what counts as just and reasonable.

The ban on family detention and on GPS ankle monitoring would remove tools immigration authorities currently use to track compliance, requiring an entirely new network of nonprofit case-management programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits fall on a heavily burdened group — incarcerated people and their families, who are a captive market for phone and money-transfer companies — while most direct costs fall on the industries profiting from incarceration. The legitimate cost is the transition burden on governments that would have to run facilities themselves, and the loss of a compliance tool in immigration enforcement. On balance the bill's design targets the specific fee structures and contracting arrangements that make detention a profit center.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and then to three subcommittees, and no committee ever scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on February 11, 2021, joined by 33 original cosponsors; the cosponsor list grew to 38, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee and additionally to Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Homeland Security.
Between February and April 2021 it was referred to the Border Security, Communications and Technology, and Crime subcommittees.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison and detention operators, prison phone and money-transfer companies, and immigration detention contractors kept their contracts, revenues, and site-commission arrangements when the bill died without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison and prison phone companies

for.name: Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 38 cosponsors, all Democrats.

for.name: 38 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the bill's cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after it was referred to his committee and then to a Judiciary subcommittee in April 2021.

against.name: Chairs of the Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Homeland Security Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; portions of it remained pending in their committees through the end of the Congress.

against.name: Private prison and prison telecom industry
against.role: CoreCivic, GEO Group, and prison phone and money-transfer providers
against.what_they_did: Maintained lobbying operations against measures to phase out for-profit confinement and cap prison phone and transfer fees during this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 House sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill also never reached a floor vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate their core business — operating prisons, jails, and ICE detention facilities for profit — within two years. Their revenue depends on charging governments per bed, a cost paid by taxpayers.

industries.industry: Prison and jail phone and video-call providers
industries.note: The bill caps their rates at 4-5 cents per minute and bans the site commissions they pay to facilities, a share of revenue that gives facilities a financial stake in charging families more.

industries.industry: Money transfer providers for correctional facilities
industries.note: Their fees for families sending money to jailed relatives would come under CFPB 'reasonable and proportional' standards, directly reducing what a captive customer base pays.
For-profit firms would be barred from operating electronic monitoring of released people, and GPS ankle monitors would be banned as an immigration detention alternative.

industries.industry: State and local governments receiving site commissions
industries.note: Governments that collect commissions from prison phone contracts would lose that revenue, but they would also gain from lower phone and transfer costs for residents in their jails.
